places.name: Little Sand Bay NPS Dock & Harbor

dock.notes: CLOSED to public slips during 2026 marina rehabilitation (sheet-piling project begins May 1, 2026); Russell boat ramp and kayak beach remain open. Shallow wood harbor dock, 3-4 ft — deep-draft boats cannot use the slips.

places.description: The park's only mainland harbor, tucked behind a small breakwall beside the historic Hokenson Brothers Fishery. It is the classic kayak jump-off for the Mawikwe sea caves and the shortest hop to Sand and York Islands, but the bay opens north and the basin runs a skinny 3-4 feet. Note the 2026 construction closure before planning a stop.
places.bestFor: Mainland base for the western islands (slips closed 2026)
places.hazards: Shoaling/sand infiltration around the harbor; the 3-7 ft Sand Cut ridge blocks any keel-boat shortcut inside Sand Island; construction activity in 2026.
funFacts: The restored Hokenson Brothers Fishery ran as a family commercial fishing operation from the 1920s to the 1960s.

places.name: East Bay (Sand Island) — Anchorage & NPS Dock

dock.fee: $15/$30 per night (6pm-6am), first-come first-served via Recreation.gov
dock.notes: Steel L-shaped dock (170 ft + 50 ft L) built 2016, repaired 2022; only 2-3 ft alongside — keel boats anchor off. Apostle Islands Cruises shuttle stop.

places.description: The classic first-night stop on a western-islands circuit, with a sand bottom, campsites ashore, and a trail to the brownstone Sand Island Lighthouse. The island wraps you from west through north, but winds famously swing 180 degrees overnight here, so be ready to shift to Justice or West Bay. Set the hook carefully — the sand can be thin over rubble.
places.bestFor: First-night stop in westerlies
places.hazards: Sand Island Shoals (least 15 ft) start 0.5 mi E of Swallow Point with the wreck of the Sevona on their east side; shoals extend 0.6 mi off the east shore; no keel-boat shortcut across the Sand Cut to the mainland.
funFacts: The 3,100-ton steamer Sevona broke up on Sand Island Shoals in a 1905 gale.
The 1881 lighthouse is built of brownstone quarried on the island itself.

places.name: Justice Bay
places.description: A clear-water sand pocket just south of Swallow Point, perfect in westerlies and famous for sea caves you can nose a dinghy into. The island kills anything from southwest through northwest, but the northeast quadrant is wide open to the lake. A favorite lunch stop that doubles as an overnight when the forecast holds westerly.
places.bestFor: Westerly-wind hook beside the Swallow Point caves
places.hazards: Sand Island Shoals and the Sevona wreck lie east of Swallow Point; sandstone ledges close inshore near the caves.
funFacts: Swallow Point is one of the park's three major sea-cave areas, with Devils Island and Mawikwe Bay.

places.name: Lighthouse Bay (Sand Island)
places.description: A small bight at Sand Island's north tip below the 1881 lighthouse, usable only when the wind has south in it. The open lake owns everything from northwest through northeast, so treat it as a lighthouse day stop and save the overnight for East or Justice Bay. Landing is on a cleated rock shelf that the NPS says demands extreme caution.
places.bestFor: Settled-southerly lighthouse day stop
places.hazards: Submerged rocks at the lighthouse landing; shoals extend up to 0.6 mi off the north shore; Sand Island Shoals to the east.
funFacts: Keeper Emmanuel Luick tended Sand Island Light for 29 years.

places.name: York Island North Beach
places.description: One of the finest beaches in the archipelago, with sailboats swinging off the sand on settled southerly nights. The low island and its southern sandspit flatten anything from southeast through west, but the Bayfield Yacht Club flags it BEWARE for good reason — the north side takes the lake's full fetch. Dinghy to the southern spit for a second, even quieter beach.
places.bestFor: Settled-southerly beach night
places.hazards: A shoal runs 0.6 mi south toward Point Detour leaving only a 0.3-mi, 20-24 ft passage; York Island Shoals (least 15 ft, buoyed) lie 2 mi NNE; shoals ring the island 0.25-0.5 mi.
funFacts: York, Sand, Raspberry and Eagle Islands were part of the mainland peninsula in preglacial times.

places.name: Raspberry Island Lighthouse Docks (West & East)

dock.notes: Two parallel steel-bin docks rebuilt 2017: West dock (5-6 ft) is effectively reserved for the excursion boat and NPS; private boats use the shallower East dock (3-4 ft).

places.description: Twin docks at Raspberry's southwest point, 76 steps below the 'showplace of the Apostles' lighthouse. The island gives a solid lee from northeast through east, but west and north winds funnel up the West Channel and put surge alongside. Favor the East dock and yield the West to the tour boat.
places.bestFor: Lighthouse day stop out of NE-E winds
places.hazards: Boulders lie east of the docks; usable depth shrinks in low-water years.

places.name: Raspberry Island Southwest Sandspit
places.description: The classic western-islands sandspit hook: anchor south of the spit in northerlies, north of it in southwesterlies, and eyeball the anchor dig in through clear water over hard rippled sand. It is heavily used and unforgiving of wind shifts — SAIL's crew famously relocated at midnight from this exact spot. Camping is prohibited on the spit itself.
places.bestFor: Pick-your-side spit lee near the lighthouse
places.hazards: Marina Shoal extends 0.4 mi south from the island's SE side; shoals 0.1-0.3 mi ring the island; wind shifts routinely force overnight moves.
funFacts: Raspberry Light (1863) is the most-visited lighthouse in the park.

places.name: Oak Island West Dock

dock.notes: Wood dock, ~6 ft at the outer end; Apostle Islands Cruises camper-shuttle stop — leave room for the excursion boat.

places.description: A wooden dock midway up Oak's west shore, hiding behind the tallest island in the park when the wind blows out of the northeast or east. Southwesterlies push channel chop and surge straight onto the face, so plan an exit. Trails to the island's 480-foot heights start right here.
places.bestFor: NE-blow dock stop with the best hiking in the park
places.hazards: Oak Island Shoal (least 18 ft) lies 0.9 mi north; shoals extend 0.3 mi off the island; resident bears — stow food afloat.
funFacts: Oak is the tallest Apostle, rising about 480 feet above the lake.

places.name: Oak Island South Sandspit
places.description: A two-sided spit at Oak's south tip: take the west side in northeast-through-southeast winds, the east side in southwest-through-north, with the island's big bluffs adding a generous wind shadow. Shallow water runs well out from the spit, so round it wide when switching sides. The cabins on the spit are private — enjoy the beach from the water.
places.bestFor: Pick-your-side spit in shifting winds
places.hazards: Spit shoal extends far offshore; Oak Island Shoal 0.9 mi north of the island; private land on the spit — no landing or camping there.
funFacts: Bears swim between Oak and the mainland often enough that food storage rules are strictly enforced.

places.name: Basswood Island West Side — Anchorage & NPS Dock

dock.notes: Steel-bin dock, shallow at 2-4 ft alongside — bigger boats anchor off. Closest island dock to Bayfield.

places.description: The nearest island stop to Bayfield, with boats anchoring in good sand right off the 70-foot dock under 100-foot brownstone shores. The island blocks easterlies nicely, but southwest and northwest winds run the length of the West Channel unimpeded. Do not tie to the old quarry rocks at the south end, tempting as their iron cleats look.
places.bestFor: Quick easterly-lee overnight nearest Bayfield
places.hazards: Submerged ruins of the quarry pier off the south end; shoals 0.2 mi off the island; ferry and excursion wakes in the channel.
amenities: loop trail to the 1868 farm and quarry
funFacts: Basswood brownstone from the 1870s quarry went into the first Milwaukee County Courthouse.

places.name: Manitou Island Fish Camp Dock

dock.fee: Overnight docking likely permitted under the park-wide 12-island $15/$30 per-night (6pm-6am) pass system — confirm the payment mechanism with the park before staying
dock.notes: Wood dock at the preserved 1930s fish camp; one of the deepest wooden island docks at 6-7 ft. Repaired 2020; replacement planned.

places.description: A good, deep wooden dock fronting the best-preserved commercial fish camp on the lake, with volunteer-led tours through the weathered 1930s buildings. The island covers you from north through east, but this is a fair-weather visit rather than a storm hole. Leave by heading straight out to deep water — the shallows toward Little Manitou are strewn with boulders.
places.bestFor: Fair-weather history stop with real depth alongside
places.hazards: Do not pass between Little Manitou shoal light and the island — very shallow; a shoal extends 0.6 mi NW from the west end.
funFacts: The camp shows how island commercial fishing operated into the mid-1900s, nets and all.

places.name: Otter Island Southeast Dock & Sandspit

dock.notes: U-shaped wood dock, 4-5 ft — deeper-draft boats anchor off the spit. Essentially the only good landing on the island.

places.description: A quiet U-shaped dock and sandspit on Otter's southeast corner — the island's one friendly landing, with the sea-cave cliffs of the northwest shore taking the punishment in northerlies. In a north or northwest blow this is a lovely, empty refuge; in anything southerly the surge finds you. Campsite 1 sits on the spit a stone's throw from the dock.
places.bestFor: NW-blow refuge with a sandspit campsite
places.hazards: Shoals run 0.4 mi off the east point and 0.2 mi elsewhere; rock-shelf landings on the rest of the island are calm-weather only; NW shore is a seasonal bird closure area.

places.name: Rocky Island East Dock

dock.notes: Wood dock, 6-7 ft — one of the deepest island docks, fronting the Rocky Island Historic District fish camps. Old private piers line this shore; confirm NPS signage on arrival.

places.description: A deep wooden dock below the preserved Hadland fish-camp cabins on Rocky's east shore, facing South Twin across a half-mile channel. It is the westerly-blow half of the archipelago's classic shelter pair — when the wind swings east, cross to South Twin's west dock. Five campsites and a seasonal ranger sit within a quarter mile.
places.bestFor: Westerly-blow dock refuge in the outer islands
places.hazards: NE wind and surge funnel straight down the channel; shoals lie 1.1 mi NE off Rocky's northeast point.

places.name: South Twin Island West Dock

dock.notes: Steel-bin dock, 4-5 ft and lake-level sensitive — a charter operator judged it unusable for keel boats in the low-water year 2024.

places.description: The easterly-blow half of the Rocky/South Twin channel pair: South Twin shields the dock from northeast through southeast while Rocky knocks down the west across the channel. Depth alongside is the catch — in low-water years keel boats should anchor in the channel instead. A seasonal ranger station and day-use area sit ashore.
places.bestFor: Easterly-blow dock refuge opposite Rocky
places.hazards: Lake-level-sensitive depths; shoal water off the dock in low-water years; channel opens south.

places.name: Rocky / South Twin Channel Anchorage
places.description: The Coast Pilot's own words: the bay between the two islands 'affords good anchorage with protection from west and northwest winds, mud bottom.' A rocky flat joining the islands' north ends breaks the northerly sea, making this the classic hurricane hole of the outer islands in a west or northwest blow. The one open door is due south along the channel axis.
places.bestFor: Outer-islands hurricane hole in W/NW blows
places.hazards: Do not exit north — the connecting rocky flat carries only ~10 ft; shoals extend 0.15 mi from both shores of the bay.
funFacts: Cruisers simply swap sides of the channel as the wind swings — Rocky's dock for westerlies, South Twin's for easterlies.

places.name: Devils Island South Landing

dock.notes: CLOSED — wrecked by the 2017 storm; Devils Island Marina Rehabilitation construction began June 2026, and marina access remains closed until construction is complete. Only 2-4 ft alongside even when open.

places.description: The only landing on the park's storm-hammered northernmost island, tucked at the south end near the old boathouse — and currently a construction zone while the 2017 storm damage is finally rebuilt. On a truly calm day, anchor off and dinghy to the sandstone flats east of the lighthouse, but the NPS warns the whole area is open to wind and surge. The legendary sea caves at the north end are strictly a flat-water treat.
places.bestFor: Calm-day sea-cave expedition base (dock closed 2026)
places.hazards: Construction zone in 2026; Devils Island Shoal (least 11 ft) 1.3 mi east; surge wraps the island even in light air; cave mouths dangerous in any wave action.
funFacts: SeaCavesWatch.org posts real-time wave data recorded at Devils Island — check it before you commit.

places.name: Michigan Island Lighthouse Dock & Anchorage

dock.fee: $15/$30 per night via Recreation.gov, though conditions rarely favor staying
dock.notes: Concrete base with a removable metal outer platform, pulled every winter since storms kept destroying fixed structures. 3-5 ft alongside; 'perfect weather only' per local operators.

places.description: A south-shore dock and near-shore sand anchorage below the only island in America with back-to-back lighthouses from 1857 and 1929. The superintendent's phrase is 'open lake exposure to all storms,' and it shows — use it in northerlies or flat calm, climb the long stairs, and leave before anything with south in it arrives.
places.bestFor: Perfect-weather double-lighthouse stop
places.hazards: Give the light a full mile berth — a 12-ft shoal spur runs 0.7 mi south; a rocky ledge covered ~2 ft runs 1.4 mi NE toward Gull Island (bird closure); open-lake surge alongside.
funFacts: The 1857 tower was reportedly built here by mistake — the contractor may have been meant to build on Long Island.

places.name: Outer Island Lighthouse Dock (North End)

dock.fee: $15/$30 overnight pass exists via Recreation.gov, but this is effectively a fair-weather day stop
dock.notes: Concrete L-pier from the Lighthouse Service era below the 1874 light; NPS warns the exposed location often makes landing impossible even when the crossing was fine.

places.description: The most remote dock in the park, a concrete L-pier under the 1874 Outer Island Light with the historic tramway still climbing the bluff behind it. Open Lake Superior surrounds it from west through north to east, and the NPS reserves this island for the most experienced boaters. Twenty-plus miles from Bayfield, no cell service, marginal VHF — plan accordingly.
places.bestFor: Settled-weather lighthouse pilgrimage
places.hazards: Shoals fringe the north end 0.5-0.6 mi out; Outer Island Shoal (least 16 ft) runs 1.2 mi north; a sunken wreck lies 1.5 mi NE of the light; no refuge within hours of sailing.
funFacts: The most remote of the six Apostle light stations, 24 miles from Bayfield.

places.name: Outer Island South Sandspit
places.bottom: sand close in, rock farther out
places.description: Perhaps the largest sandspit in the islands, with mile-long dune beaches running up both sides — the signature remote anchorage of the Apostles. Anchor tight to the spit on the lee side in good sand; farther out the bottom turns to rock and one forum crew rode out 46-knot gusts hoping their hook stayed put. There is no all-weather protection here and no bailout nearby, so watch the forecast like a hawk.
places.bestFor: Remote dune anchorage in settled weather
places.hazards: Rocky bank 0.4 mi off the southwest point; extreme remoteness — NPS recommends only the most experienced boaters attempt Outer; weather can strand you far from shelter.
funFacts: The dunes run 10-40 feet high for a mile along both sides of the spit.

places.name: Presque Isle Bay (Stockton Island)

dock.fee: $15/$30 per night (6pm-6am) via Recreation.gov; strictly first-come first-served
dock.notes: Two-pier concrete complex (West dock 6-7 ft, East dock 4-7 ft) behind breakwalls — the deepest and largest dock complex in the park. Significant space reserved for NPS and cruise vessels; tie only in unreserved sections.

places.description: The busiest and best anchorage in the archipelago, cradled by Stockton's landmass, the Presque Isle tombolo, and the park's only breakwall harbor — calm and secure even on windy days from every direction but south. Drop the hook in clear water over hard rippled sand, watch it set, then walk Singing Sands Beach or grab a slip at the deepest docks in the park. Only a strong southerly blow pushes swell into the bay.
places.bestFor: All-around refuge; the park's only true harbor
places.hazards: Shoals extend ~0.4 mi off Stockton's east end; dramatic wind shifts are common — a hard southerly can make the open bay rough; docks fill fast in July-August.
funFacts: Presque Isle was once a separate island, joined to Stockton by the tombolo whose sandspit forms the harbor.
Cruising World counted sailboats outnumbering powerboats here nearly 10 to 1.

places.name: Quarry Bay (Stockton Island)

dock.fee: $15/$30 per night (6pm-6am) via separate 'Stockton Quarry Bay' Recreation.gov pass
dock.notes: Rebuilt wood dock, 5-6 ft, fronting the beach on the bay's north side; limited space.

places.description: Presque Isle's quieter neighbor on Stockton's southwest shore: same fine sand holding, fewer boats, and a beachfront dock with a trail to the abandoned 1896 brownstone quarry. The island seals off everything from west through north to east, but the bay lies open to the southern quadrant — when the forecast swings southerly, slide around to Presque Isle.
places.bestFor: Northerly-blow anchorage with a quarry hike
places.hazards: Southerly surge alongside the dock; remnant quarry stonework ashore; wind shifts common.
funFacts: The quarry shut down in 1896 with cut blocks and machinery abandoned in place — they are still there.

places.name: Julian Bay (Stockton Island)
places.description: The east side of the Presque Isle tombolo, where the famous singing sands squeak underfoot and the water shelves out gently over clean sand. It is glorious in a westerly and untenable in any easterly, so most boats day-anchor here and hop over the tombolo — or around it — to sleep in Presque Isle Bay. Snorkelers can visit the burned wreck of the Noquebay just offshore.
places.bestFor: Southerly-or-westerly beach day on singing sands
places.hazards: Wide open to NE-E-SE seas; the schooner-barge Noquebay (1905) is a protected historic site at 46.9261, -90.5453 — do not anchor on the wreck; shoals off Stockton's east end.
funFacts: The squeak of Julian Bay's sand comes from uniform quartz grains rubbing — hence 'singing sands.'

places.name: Cat Island South Sandspit
places.description: A textbook pick-your-side spit in the quiet middle islands: west side for northeast-through-southeast winds, east side for southwest-through-north. The spit's submerged tail runs a full 0.6 miles south, so swing wide when you change sides. Boat-campers love the forest site behind the spit and the zone camping along the northeast beach.
places.bestFor: Quiet middle-islands spit, either-side lee
places.hazards: 0.6-mi shoal running south off the spit; shoals 0.3-0.5 mi around the north end; the Waterway Guide pin sits erroneously at the island's north tip — the anchorage is at the south spit.
funFacts: Rugged sea caves line Cat Island's north end.

places.name: Ironwood Island South Sandspit
places.description: A partially protected spit anchorage off a nearly round, mile-wide island that most cruisers sail right past. Tuck onto whichever side of the spit the wind favors and you will likely have it entirely to yourself. Campers rate the spit campsite among the prettiest in the whole park.
places.bestFor: Solitude on a picture-perfect spit
places.hazards: Fringing shoals 0.2-0.4 mi all around; untenable in strong southerlies.
amenities: sandspit campsite with fire ring and food locker
funFacts: Friends of the Apostle Islands called the spit campsite 'perfection defined.'

places.name: Frog Bay (Mainland — Red Cliff)
places.description: A quiet mainland pocket where the wooded Bayfield Peninsula shore rises straight out of the water and kills any southerly sea. The Bayfield Yacht Club sends boats here in south, southwest, and west winds; the pristine beach at the Frog Creek mouth belongs to Frog Bay Tribal National Park — the first tribal national park in the United States. Day use only ashore, and respect Red Cliff Band rules.
places.bestFor: Mainland lee in S-SW-W blows
places.hazards: Open to N-NE; a sunken wreck lies close to shore on the north side of Red Cliff Bay nearby, and the steamer Fedora (1901) lies 0.45 mi NE of the Buffalo Bay breakwater.
amenities: views of Oak, Basswood, Hermit and Raspberry
funFacts: Frog Bay Tribal National Park (2012) was the first tribal national park in the U.S.

places.name: Eagle Bay (Mainland)
places.description: A local-knowledge bight tucked just east of Point Detour, recommended by the Bayfield Yacht Club for southeast through southwest winds when the peninsula bluffs give a clean lee. It is documented only in the club's anchorage table, so sound your way in and verify swing room. Not to be confused with Eagle Island, the closed bird sanctuary nine miles west.
places.bestFor: Local-knowledge southerly lee near the York passage
places.hazards: The York-mainland passage a mile east is only 0.3 mi wide with 20-24 ft between shoals; open to N-NE.
amenities: rustic tribal campground ashore at Point Detour

places.name: Raspberry Bay (Mainland)
places.description: The widest-ranging mainland refuge in the western islands: pocketed between Point Detour and Raspberry Point, the Bayfield Yacht Club rates it for east, southeast, south, southwest, AND west winds. Only the north-northeast door is open, and Raspberry Island 2.2 miles offshore takes some sting out of even that. When hard southerly-through-westerly weather makes the island anchorages untenable, this is where the fleet goes.
places.bestFor: Go-to mainland refuge in S-through-W blows
places.hazards: Give Raspberry Point a fair berth — Marina Shoal off Raspberry Island's SE side lies across the northern approach; Red Cliff reservation shoreline ashore.

places.name: Mawikwe Bay Sea Caves (Mainland) — Day Stop Only
places.island: Mainland — Meyers Beach to Sand Point
places.bottom: sand with boulder fields under collapsed cliff faces
places.description: The park's longest sea-cave system, carved into a northwest-facing cliff shore that takes the full fetch of western Lake Superior — this is a flat-calm, daylight-only stop, never an overnight. Anchor off temporarily in settled weather, avoid the boulder patches, and explore by dinghy or kayak; surge lingers at the cave mouths long after the wind dies. On a good day expect dozens of guided paddlers.
places.bestFor: Flat-calm sea-cave day visit only
places.hazards: Cliff-collapse boulders close inshore; swell reflection capsizes small craft at the cave mouths; no refuge for 6+ miles between Cornucopia and Little Sand Bay.
funFacts: In hard winters these same caves become the famous walkable 'ice caves' reached from Meyers Beach.

places.name: Eagle Island — Wildlife Closure (No Anchorage)
places.description: Not an anchorage — a hazard and exclusion flag. Boats must stay at least 500 feet off Eagle Island from May 15 to September 1 to protect nesting colonial birds, and outside those dates the shoal-girt, fully exposed islet still offers nothing to a cruiser. Eagle Island Shoals (least 12 ft) sprawl 1.5 miles to its southwest.
places.bestFor: Avoid — seasonal 500-ft wildlife buffer and shoals
places.hazards: Shoals extend 0.25-0.8 mi in all directions; a gravel-and-boulder ledge near the southern shoals shows only in storms; westernmost Apostle with no refuge nearby.
funFacts: Eagle and Gull Islands together host 88% of the park's breeding herring gulls.

places.name: Gull Island — Wildlife Closure (No Anchorage)
places.description: Do not anchor or approach: Gull Island is closed to visitors year-round, and boats must stay 500 feet off from May 15 to September 1. The three-acre islet sits mid-way along a rocky ledge running northeast from Michigan Island that is covered by only about two feet of water — pass well east and north. Included purely as an exclusion-zone and hazard flag.
places.bestFor: Avoid — year-round bird sanctuary and 2-ft ledge
places.hazards: Ledge between Gull and Michigan covered ~2 ft; boulders just under the surface all around; Gull Island Shoal (least 18 ft) 3.6 mi NE; 500-ft buffer May 15-Sep 1.
funFacts: The shallow reef around Gull is an important native fish spawning site.

places.name: Big Bay (Madeline Island)
places.description: A mile-and-a-half crescent of state-park beach backed by bluffs, with deep water running to within a tenth of a mile of the bay's head so you can tuck well in. Superb on a settled westerly; leave promptly if the wind backs anywhere east of north, because the open lake owns that whole quadrant. Madeline is the only inhabited Apostle, and the lagoon boardwalk ashore is worth the dinghy ride.
places.bestFor: Settled-westerly beach day off the state park
places.hazards: Open-lake exposure to any easterly; shoals extend 0.9 mi around Madeline's east point on the approach from the north.
amenities: Big Bay State Park beach and boardwalk
funFacts: Madeline is the only Apostle outside the National Lakeshore — and the only one with a year-round town.

places.name: La Pointe Special Anchorage (Madeline Island)
places.description: A federally designated special anchorage (33 CFR 110.77b) just southeast of La Pointe Harbor, where anchored boats are even exempt from showing anchor lights. Madeline blocks the north and east, the Bayfield Peninsula tempers the west, and town, marina, and ferry dock are a short dinghy ride away. Mind the sub-6-foot shoal running half a mile off Grants Point and the steady ferry wakes.
places.bestFor: Town anchorage a dinghy ride from La Pointe
places.hazards: Buoyed shoal (<6 ft) extends 0.5 mi SW of Grants Point; Bayfield-La Pointe ferries cross constantly; most exposed SW down the South Channel.
amenities: Madeline Island Marina and ferry nearby
funFacts: Grants Point fronts one of the oldest continuously occupied sites on the Great Lakes.

places.name: Bayfield Marina

dock.fee: Transient dockage; historic guest rate ~$1.25-1.50/ft/night (25 ft min); reservations via MarinaGo
dock.notes: ~190-211 fixed slips behind the city breakwall; city-run since the BD Marine lease ended December 2023 (formerly Apostle Islands Marina). Phone 715-779-1078, VHF 16.

places.description: The downtown Bayfield basin behind the city breakwall, steps from restaurants, groceries, and the whole hum of the Apostles' home port. Full fuel dock with ethanol-free gas and diesel, pumpout, service yard, and a ship store make it the default provisioning stop. Some directories still list it under its old Apostle Islands Marina name.
places.bestFor: Full-service home-port base for the islands
funFacts: The city projected roughly $100,000 a year in new income when it took over marina operations.

places.name: Bayfield City Dock

dock.fee: Published 2021 rates: $31/night (25 ft and under), +$1/ft by length — verify current rates; non-reservable, first-come first-served
dock.notes: 30 slips plus side ties for boats 25 ft and up at the foot of Rittenhouse Ave; no fuel or pumpout here — use Bayfield Marina next door. Phone 715-779-1078.

places.description: The city's own transient wall at the foot of Rittenhouse Avenue, inside the same breakwall as the marina and even closer to downtown. First-come first-served with water and power, it is the cheap-and-cheerful way to sleep in the heart of the 'Gateway to the Apostle Islands.' A 2026 finger-pier rebuild is adding capacity for larger boats.
places.bestFor: Walk-to-dinner transient wall in downtown Bayfield

places.name: Pikes Bay Marina
places.island: Mainland — Pikes Bay, south of Bayfield

dock.notes: 208 floating slips 30-60 ft, side ties to 90 ft, behind a black granite breakwall; ValvTect gas and diesel, 35-ton travelift, heated indoor storage.

places.description: A deep-draft, weather-safe basin behind a black granite breakwall three miles south of Bayfield, sharing Pikes Bay with Port Superior. Wide floating piers, 100-amp three-phase power, a clubhouse with a full kitchen, and a serious service yard make it the polished big-boat option. Wave action inside is minimal by design.
places.bestFor: Protected floating-dock base with premium services

places.name: Port Superior Marina
places.island: Mainland — Pikes Bay, south of Bayfield

dock.fee: Transient $2.00/ft/day, $10/ft/week, $30/ft/month; 12 transient slips; 715-779-5360, VHF 16, or Dockwa
dock.notes: 211 slips to 66 ft in an 'extremely well protected harbor'; transient guests get full resort amenities.

places.description: A resort-style marina in the same well-protected Pikes Bay pocket as its neighbor, two miles south of Bayfield. Beyond the usual fuel, pumpout, and travelift, transients get the pool, restaurant, and lodging of the surrounding resort. Liveaboards and pets welcome.
places.bestFor: Resort amenities with your transient slip

places.name: Madeline Island Yacht Club

dock.fee: Transient $1.75/ft/day, $10.50/ft/week (2020 card); 13-15 transient slips 25-80 ft; 715-747-2655, VHF 16, or Dockwa
dock.notes: 176-slip member cooperative (organized 1977) whose 'very well protected' docks welcome non-members space-available; 35-ton travelift; separate small-boat harbor.

places.description: A well-sheltered cooperative basin a short walk from the village of La Pointe, with premium ethanol-free gas at the service dock and the largest ship store in the Chequamegon Bay area. Non-members are welcome on a space-available basis, and the ferry to Bayfield leaves from just up the shore. The island-side alternative to a Bayfield slip.
places.bestFor: Island-side full-service base by La Pointe village
funFacts: The club's ship store doubles as the area's largest, stocking camping and beach gear for island visitors.

places.name: Roys Point Marina

dock.notes: 42 slips to 55 ft on the West Channel opposite Basswood Island; shorepower and water at every slip; breakwall construction undocumented — verify protection locally.

places.description: A small, personable 42-slip basin on the West Channel three miles north of Bayfield, with Basswood Island framing the view and a natural beach next door. Every slip has power and water, and the clubhouse decks are made for sunset. The closest marina to the heart of the islands.
places.bestFor: Small quiet basin closest to the inner islands

places.name: Buffalo Bay Marina (Legendary Waters)

dock.notes: 45 floating slips 25-50 ft behind the Buffalo Bay breakwater at Legendary Waters Resort & Casino, run by the Red Cliff Band; NO fuel or pumpout — plan fuel at Bayfield or Pikes Bay. Season May-October.

places.description: The Red Cliff Band's floating-dock basin below Legendary Waters Resort & Casino, with a sandy swimming beach on one side and a casino restaurant on the other. A flat $35 overnight makes it one of the best slip deals on the water, but carry your fuel plans elsewhere. Wisconsin Clean Marina certified.
places.bestFor: Budget slip with casino and beach attached
places.hazards: The burned steamer Fedora (1901) lies 0.45 mi NE of the breakwater basin.
amenities: electric and water at most slips

places.name: Schooner Bay Marina

dock.fee: ~$2.00/ft transient; 3 transient slips; 715-779-3266 — call ahead, listings are sparse and dated
dock.notes: 40-45 floating slips off Pageant Road; liveaboard and DIY repairs permitted; fuel not documented.

places.description: A small private marina tucked into Schooner Bay north of Red Cliff, the last mainland slips before the open run to the western islands. Data on it is thin and some listings are stale, so phone ahead before counting on a transient berth. Handy 30-amp power, showers, and a workshop for boats that fix themselves.
places.bestFor: Low-key private slips nearest the western run

places.name: Washburn Marina

dock.notes: 138 slips 24-50 ft (boats to ~110 ft), protected dockage on Chequamegon Bay's west shore; big travel lift and full repair yard for pleasure and small commercial craft.

places.description: A working full-service yard on Chequamegon Bay's west shore, eleven miles from Bayfield, where cruisers go when something actually needs fixing — the travel lift is one of the biggest in the region. Protected dockage, fuel, and the town of Washburn a short walk away. A sensible provisioning or repair detour rather than an islands base.
places.bestFor: Repairs, haul-out, and provisioning on the bay

places.name: Siskiwit Bay Marina (Cornucopia)

dock.notes: 65 fixed and floating slips at the Siskiwit River mouth — Wisconsin's northernmost harbor; 30,000-lb travel lift, full repairs, family-run.

places.description: Wisconsin's northernmost harbor and the western gateway to the Apostles, a family-run 65-slip marina in the artsy fishing hamlet of Cornucopia. It is the last stop before the Mawikwe sea caves four miles east and the only refuge on the long exposed stretch west of Sand Island. Groceries, taverns, and a beach are all a short walk from your slip.
places.bestFor: Western gateway and sea-cave staging harbor
funFacts: 'Corny' bills itself as Wisconsin's northernmost post office.

places.name: Ashland Marina

dock.fee: 15 transient slips for boats to 55 ft; 715-682-7049, VHF 16
dock.notes: 121 floating slips with side-tie capability at the foot of Ellis Avenue; closed November-March; fuel, pumpout, and a dock attendant on duty.

places.description: The city marina at the head of Chequamegon Bay, twenty miles from Bayfield and sheltered from the open lake by the whole length of the bay. Floating docks, fuel, and downtown Ashland's shops within walking distance make it a solid provisioning stop, though the bay's own northerly fetch can kick up a chop at the entrance. More a friendly waypoint than an Apostles base.
places.bestFor: Provisioning stop at the head of the bay

places.name: Saxon Harbor Marina & Campground

dock.notes: 81-93 slips rebuilt after the 2016 flash flood destroyed the harbor (~$14M, reopened 2019); Army Corps-designated harbor of refuge; entrance rated only 'fair' for marking — take care in poor visibility.

places.description: An engineered county harbor of refuge at the Oronto Creek mouth, roughly 25 miles east-southeast of Madeline Island and the only real shelter between Chequamegon Bay and the Michigan line. Completely rebuilt after the 2016 flash flood scattered its fleet into the lake, it now pairs sturdy breakwalls with a creekside campground. Eastbound Apostles cruisers should keep it in their pocket.
places.bestFor: Harbor of refuge on the eastbound run
places.hazards: Entrance marking and maneuverability rated only 'fair'; history of extreme flash-flood outwash from Oronto and Parker Creeks.
funFacts: The 2016 storm dropped nearly 10 inches of rain in 12 hours; the rebuilt harbor reopened three years later.
